knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, fig.align = "center")

> **In this step** we download the public ImmVar expression data from GEO, build a
> table that describes every array, decide which donors to analyse, and save a
> clean, log2-scale expression matrix for the modelling step.
>
> **Reads:** `data/source_files.csv` (download links and checksums)<br>
> **Writes:** `data/processed/immvar.rds` and six tables in `results/tables/`<br>
> **Run time:** under a minute, plus a one-time ~90 MB download

# Background

The ImmVar project measured gene expression in two immune cell types, naïve CD4
T cells and monocytes, from several hundred healthy donors. The data are
public in GEO as series [GSE56035](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE56035),
measured on Affymetrix Human Gene 1.0 ST arrays (GEO platform
[GPL6244](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GPL6244)).

The question for the whole analysis is:

> For each probe, how much of the variation in expression is associated with
> **cell type**, **donor**, **age**, **sex** and **processing batch**?

This first notebook only prepares the data. Steps 2–4 fit the models and
interpret the results.

# Setup

The project keeps its packages in a local `library/` folder (created by
`install_packages.R`) so it never changes your system-wide R installation.

```{r packages}
.libPaths(c("library", .libPaths()))
library(data.table)  # fast reading and writing of large tables
library(ggplot2)     # plots

options(timeout = 600)  # allow up to 10 minutes for each GEO download

# Create every output folder used by the four notebooks.
for (folder in c("data/raw", "data/processed", "results/tables",
                 "results/models", "results/figures")) {
  dir.create(folder, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
}
```

# Download the GEO files

We need two files:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `GSE56035_series_matrix.txt.gz` | Expression values **and** the sample information (age, sex, cell type, batch) |
| `GPL6244.annot.gz` | Platform annotation, which maps each probe ID to a gene symbol |

Their web addresses and MD5 checksums are stored in `data/source_files.csv`. A
checksum is a fingerprint of the file: if GEO ever changes a file, or a download
is cut short, the fingerprint will not match and the notebook stops rather than
silently analysing different data.

```{r download}
sources <- read.csv("data/source_files.csv")

for (i in seq_len(nrow(sources))) {
  path <- file.path("data/raw", sources$file[i])

  # Download only if we do not already have the file.
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    download.file(sources$url[i], path, mode = "wb", method = "libcurl")
  }

  # Stop if the file is not exactly the version this analysis was built on.
  if (unname(tools::md5sum(path)) != sources$md5[i]) {
    stop("The GEO file differs from the version used here: ", path,
         ". Check it before updating data/source_files.csv.")
  }
}

sources[, c("file", "md5")]
```

# Read the sample information

## How a GEO series matrix is laid out

A series matrix is a plain-text file with two parts:

1. **A header.** Each line starts with `!`. Lines that begin with `!Sample_`
   hold one tab-separated value per array, such as its ID, title or donor age.
2. **The expression table.** This sits between the lines
   `!series_matrix_table_begin` and `!series_matrix_table_end`. Its rows are
   probes and its columns are arrays.

We first read just the header, stopping at the start of the table.

```{r read-header}
connection <- gzfile("data/raw/GSE56035_series_matrix.txt.gz", "rt")
header <- character()
repeat {
  line <- readLines(connection, n = 1)
  if (!length(line)) stop("Could not find the expression table.")
  if (line == "!series_matrix_table_begin") break
  header <- c(header, line)
}
close(connection)

length(header)  # number of header lines
```

The sample characteristics are stored as `label: value` text. Here are the
first few characters of each characteristics line, so you can see the format:

```{r peek-characteristics}
characteristic_lines <- header[startsWith(header, "!Sample_characteristics_ch1\t")]
substr(characteristic_lines, 1, 80)
```

## Two small helper functions

* `read_field()` returns the values of one named header line, such as
  `!Sample_geo_accession`, with one value per array.
* `read_characteristic()` finds the characteristics line whose label matches a
  pattern, such as `"^batch:"`, and strips the label to keep only the value.

Both helpers stop with an error if they do not find **exactly one** matching
line. This guards against silently picking up the wrong field.

```{r helpers}
read_field <- function(name) {
  line <- header[startsWith(header, paste0(name, "\t"))]
  stopifnot(length(line) == 1)
  scan(text = line, what = "", sep = "\t", quote = '"', quiet = TRUE)[-1]
}

# Split every characteristics line into one value per array.
characteristics <- lapply(characteristic_lines, function(line) {
  scan(text = line, what = "", sep = "\t", quote = '"', quiet = TRUE)[-1]
})

read_characteristic <- function(pattern) {
  found <- vapply(characteristics,
                  function(x) any(grepl(pattern, x, ignore.case = TRUE)),
                  logical(1))
  stopifnot(sum(found) == 1)
  sub("^[^:]+: *", "", characteristics[[which(found)]])  # drop "label: "
}
```

## Build the sample table

We now build `metadata`, with **one row per array**. The donor ID
(`Individual`) is the part of the sample title before the first dot. The same
donor therefore has the same ID on their T-cell and monocyte arrays, which is
what links a person's two cell types together.

```{r build-metadata}
metadata <- data.frame(
  sample_id = read_field("!Sample_geo_accession"),
  title     = read_field("!Sample_title"),
  Age       = as.numeric(read_characteristic("^age ")),
  Sex       = tools::toTitleCase(tolower(read_characteristic("^(sex|gender):"))),
  CellType  = ifelse(grepl("monocyte", read_characteristic("^cell type:"),
                           ignore.case = TRUE),
                     "Monocyte", "CD4_T"),
  Batch     = read_characteristic("^batch:")
)
metadata$Individual <- sub("\\..*$", "", metadata$title)

# Sanity checks: nothing missing, IDs unique, donor IDs look like "IGTB123".
stopifnot(!anyNA(metadata),
          !anyDuplicated(metadata$sample_id),
          all(grepl("^IGTB[0-9]+$", metadata$Individual)))

head(metadata)
```

# Choose which donors to analyse

The models in Step 2 separate **cell type** from **donor**. To do that cleanly,
each donor must contribute arrays from **both** cell types. We also require
each donor to have a single recorded age and a single recorded sex across their
arrays. If the records disagree, we cannot know which value is correct, so we
leave the donor out rather than guess.

We first summarise each donor:

```{r donor-summary}
donors <- as.data.table(metadata)[, .(
  n_arrays      = .N,                   # arrays from this donor
  n_cell_types  = uniqueN(CellType),    # 1 or 2
  n_ages        = uniqueN(Age),         # should be 1
  n_sexes       = uniqueN(Sex),         # should be 1
  recorded_ages = paste(sort(unique(Age)), collapse = ";")
), by = Individual]

donors[, paired   := n_cell_types == 2]
donors[, included := paired & n_ages == 1 & n_sexes == 1]

donors[, .N, by = .(paired, included)]
```

The paired donors we exclude all have **conflicting ages** recorded on
different arrays:

```{r excluded-donors}
donors[paired & !included]
```

Next we copy the `paired` and `included` flags onto every array. We also turn
the grouping columns into factors, because the models treat them as
categories.

```{r flag-arrays}
metadata$paired   <- donors$paired[match(metadata$Individual, donors$Individual)]
metadata$included <- donors$included[match(metadata$Individual, donors$Individual)]

for (name in c("Sex", "CellType", "Batch", "Individual")) {
  metadata[[name]] <- factor(metadata[[name]])
}
rownames(metadata) <- metadata$sample_id

fwrite(donors,   "results/tables/donor_qc.csv")
fwrite(metadata, "results/tables/sample_metadata.csv")
```

## A look at the analysis cohort

```{r cohort}
cohort <- metadata[metadata$included, ]

# Arrays per cell type and sex
table(CellType = cohort$CellType, Sex = cohort$Sex)

# How many arrays does each donor have? (2 = one per cell type)
as.data.frame(table(arrays_per_donor = table(droplevels(cohort$Individual))))
```

Most donors have one array per cell type. A few have repeat arrays. Because
the same person appears several times, arrays from one donor are not
independent, and Step 2 models this with a donor term.

```{r age-plot, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3}
donor_info <- unique(cohort[, c("Individual", "Age", "Sex")])

ggplot(donor_info, aes(Age, fill = Sex)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ Sex) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Donors",
       title = "Age of the analysed donors") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

# Read the expression matrix

`fread()` reads large tables quickly. It can only read a `.gz` file directly if
an extra package is installed, so we decompress the file to a temporary copy
first. We skip the header lines and read exactly the number of probe rows that
GEO reports.

```{r read-expression}
connection <- gzfile("data/raw/GSE56035_series_matrix.txt.gz", "rb")
temporary  <- tempfile(fileext = ".txt")
output     <- file(temporary, "wb")
repeat {
  block <- readBin(connection, "raw", n = 1024 * 1024)  # 1 MB at a time
  if (!length(block)) break
  writeBin(block, output)
}
close(connection)
close(output)

table <- fread(temporary,
               skip  = length(header) + 1,
               nrows = as.integer(read_field("!Sample_data_row_count")[1]))
unlink(temporary)

# Turn the table into a numeric matrix: rows = probes, columns = arrays.
probe_ids  <- as.character(table[[1]])
expression <- as.matrix(table[, -1])
storage.mode(expression) <- "double"
rownames(expression) <- probe_ids

# The columns must be in the same order as the rows of `metadata`.
stopifnot(identical(colnames(expression), metadata$sample_id),
          !anyDuplicated(probe_ids),
          all(is.finite(expression)))

dim(expression)       # probes x arrays
expression[1:5, 1:4]  # top-left corner
```

# Check for batch effects

Arrays were processed in batches, and batch-to-batch technical differences are
a common problem in expression data. Before changing anything, we ask how much
of each probe's variation the recorded batch labels can explain.

For each probe and each cell type, we regress expression on batch and record
the **R²**, the fraction of variance explained. A batch factor with many levels
always explains *some* variance by chance. To show what chance alone looks like,
we repeat the calculation with **shuffled** batch labels. If the real R² is
close to the shuffled R², the recorded batches carry little real signal.

```{r batch-check}
# R-squared of `values` (probes x arrays) on `batch`, for every probe at once.
batch_r2 <- function(values, batch) {
  y     <- t(values)                                 # arrays x probes
  fit   <- lm.fit(model.matrix(~ batch), y)          # one regression per probe
  total <- colSums(sweep(y, 2, colMeans(y))^2)       # total sum of squares
  1 - colSums(fit$residuals^2) / total
}

set.seed(20261104)  # makes the shuffled labels reproducible
batch_checks <- list()
for (cell in unique(as.character(metadata$CellType))) {
  samples <- metadata$CellType == cell
  batch   <- droplevels(metadata$Batch[samples])
  batch_checks[[cell]] <- data.frame(
    probe_id    = probe_ids,
    cell_type   = cell,
    observed_r2 = batch_r2(expression[, samples], batch),
    shuffled_r2 = batch_r2(expression[, samples], sample(batch))
  )
}
batch_structure <- do.call(rbind, batch_checks)
fwrite(batch_structure, "results/tables/batch_structure.csv")
```

```{r batch-summary}
batch_summary <- as.data.table(batch_structure)[, .(
  median_r2_real_labels     = median(observed_r2),
  median_r2_shuffled_labels = median(shuffled_r2),
  percent_probes_real_below_shuffled = 100 * mean(observed_r2 < shuffled_r2)
), by = cell_type]
batch_summary
```

```{r batch-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
batch_long <- melt(as.data.table(batch_structure),
                   id.vars = c("probe_id", "cell_type"),
                   variable.name = "labels", value.name = "r2")

ggplot(batch_long, aes(r2, colour = labels)) +
  geom_density() +
  facet_wrap(~ cell_type) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(observed_r2 = "#1F78B4", shuffled_r2 = "grey50"),
                      labels = c("Real batch labels", "Shuffled labels")) +
  labs(x = "R² explained by batch, per probe (log scale)", y = "Density",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**How to read this.** If batches had introduced technical differences, the
blue curve (real labels) would sit to the **right** of the grey one, because
real batches would explain more than random groupings. Here it sits far to the
**left**. The real batch labels explain *less* variance than shuffled labels for
`r round(min(batch_summary$percent_probes_real_below_shuffled), 1)`% or more of
probes. This is the pattern you would expect if batch had already been removed
before the data were deposited in GEO, although the full processing history is
unknown. We apply **no** further batch correction. Step 2 still includes batch
in the model, so any batch variation that remains is measured.

# Convert to log2 scale and remove problem probes

GEO describes these values as RMA output "on 2^ scale". RMA normally produces
log2 values, so here they have been converted back to the linear scale. We take
`log2()` to return to the usual log scale.

A logarithm is only defined for positive numbers, yet some probes contain zero
or negative values. Rather than clip those values or add an arbitrary
pseudocount, we **remove any probe that has a nonpositive value on any array**.

```{r log-transform}
# Confirm GEO describes every array as "Output on 2^ scale".
stopifnot(all(grepl("Output on 2\\^ scale", read_field("!Sample_data_processing"))))

probe_qc <- data.frame(probe_id      = probe_ids,
                       n_nonpositive = rowSums(expression <= 0))
keep_probe <- probe_qc$n_nonpositive == 0
probe_qc$included <- keep_probe

expression <- log2(expression[keep_probe, ])

# Every remaining probe must actually vary across the analysed arrays.
stopifnot(all(apply(expression[, metadata$included], 1, var) > 1e-8))
fwrite(probe_qc, "results/tables/probe_qc.csv")

c(probes_removed = sum(!keep_probe), probes_kept = sum(keep_probe))
```

# Add gene annotation

Probe IDs are numbers, such as `8157524`. The platform annotation file tells us
which gene each probe measures. We keep the **probe** as the unit of analysis
and do not average probes into genes, because some probes map to several genes
(shown as `A /// B`) or to none. The annotation is only there to help us
interpret the results.

```{r annotation}
connection <- gzfile("data/raw/GPL6244.annot.gz", "rt")
lines <- readLines(connection)
close(connection)

# The probe table sits between these two marker lines.
start <- which(lines == "!platform_table_begin") + 1
end   <- which(lines == "!platform_table_end") - 1
platform <- fread(text = paste(lines[start:end], collapse = "\n"),
                  sep = "\t", quote = "", fill = TRUE)
platform <- platform[match(probe_ids, as.character(platform$ID)), ]

annotation <- data.frame(
  probe_id   = probe_ids,
  symbol     = platform[["Gene symbol"]],
  gene_title = platform[["Gene title"]],
  gene_id    = platform[["Gene ID"]]
)
annotation$symbol[is.na(annotation$symbol) | annotation$symbol == ""] <- NA_character_
annotation$unique_symbol <- !is.na(annotation$symbol) &
  !grepl("///", annotation$symbol, fixed = TRUE)
fwrite(annotation, "results/tables/probe_annotation.csv")

# The three probes used as examples later in the analysis:
subset(annotation, probe_id %in% c("8157524", "8177232", "7903765"),
       select = c(probe_id, symbol, gene_title))
```

# Save the prepared data

Everything the next steps need is saved in one R object:

* `expression`: log2 expression matrix (probes × **all** arrays)
* `metadata`: one row per array, including the `included` flag
* `annotation`: probe-to-gene table

All arrays are kept in the saved file, and the `included` flag marks the
analysis cohort. This lets the sensitivity analysis in Step 4 use a slightly
larger set of donors.

```{r save}
saveRDS(list(expression = expression, metadata = metadata, annotation = annotation),
        "data/processed/immvar.rds", compress = FALSE)

counts <- data.frame(
  item = c("Input arrays", "Input probes", "Donor prefixes", "Paired donors",
           "Primary donors", "Primary arrays", "Retained probes"),
  n    = c(nrow(metadata), length(probe_ids), nrow(donors), sum(donors$paired),
           sum(donors$included), sum(metadata$included), nrow(expression))
)
fwrite(counts, "results/tables/sample_counts.csv")
counts
```

# Summary

* Starting from **`r format(nrow(metadata), big.mark = ",")` arrays** and
  **`r format(length(probe_ids), big.mark = ",")` probes**, the analysis keeps
  **`r sum(donors$included)` donors** with both cell types and consistent
  records, which gives **`r sum(metadata$included)` arrays**.
* **`r format(nrow(expression), big.mark = ",")` probes** remain after
  removing those with nonpositive values. Expression is now on the log2 scale.
* The recorded batch labels explain even less variance than shuffled labels,
  which suggests batch was already adjusted for before the data reached GEO.
